In these conditions, active control placed 92.9\% of valid altitude samples within $\pm500$\,mm of the 1000\,mm target, compared with 80.7\% for the adjusted passive configuration (Table~\ref{tab:ocean_results}). The time-in-band statistics reported by \textcite{lembke_cbass} provide context, but differing altitude bands, operating conditions and treatment of invalid samples preclude a direct ranking of performance. The passive rope was shortened to suit the local depth, while the active run required no reported rope adjustment during towing; these are operationally different configurations.

Within the band, RMS error was nearly identical (195.2\,mm passive and 192.9\,mm active). The passive mean in-band error was $+10.8$\,mm. Active control had an in-band standard deviation of approximately 124\,mm and mean error of $+147.7$\,mm, indicating lower scatter with an above-target bias in this selected subset. Limited nose-down authority is a possible explanation for the active offset, but the simulation result alone does not establish that cause in the ocean trial. Logged fin saturation, pitch error and integral state would be needed to test it. Subtracting the observed mean would reduce RMS towards 124\,mm only if the same samples and variability were retained; this is a mathematical decomposition, not demonstrated controller performance.

The central 95\% of in-band samples extended from 833 to 1457\,mm for active control and 581 to 1403\,mm for the passive configuration. Across all valid samples, RMS error was 288.9\,mm active and 363.2\,mm passive. Invalid readings, logged as 0\,mm when no echo was received, constituted 14.3\% and 37.6\% of all samples, respectively. Possible causes include operation beyond the approximately 2\,m practical sensor range and beam orientations that lost the seabed (Section~\ref{sec:Exp5}); the trial did not distinguish these mechanisms.

Using all logged samples as the denominator, approximately 79.6\% of active samples and 50.3\% of passive samples were both valid and within the band. Invalid samples represent unknown clearance and do not demonstrate either seabed contact or an excursion outside the band. These availability measures therefore differ from verified physical time-in-band. All experimental error metrics use the rig's own altitude estimate; no independent altitude reference was recorded, so absolute clearance accuracy remains unverified.

The active trace appears less variable over much of the plotted interval, but the cause of individual excursions and run termination cannot be established from these plots alone. One run per configuration, different rope lengths, unequal durations and uncontrolled environmental differences limit attribution of the observed differences to the controller. The comparison provides preliminary evidence favouring active regulation rather than a statistically established improvement.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This project investigated whether a low-cost, predominantly 3D-printed tow camera could hold a stable, low altitude above the seabed using ultrasonic sensing and active fin control, as a platform for automated Caulerpa survey. The rig was developed over six experiments and a software-in-the-loop simulation. The scale model confirmed the diving mechanism, the full-scale trials fixed the tow point and sensing, and simulation supported replacement of the oscillatory single-loop PID controller with a cascaded PI--P controller that approached and crossed the target altitude during a short pool run.

Control authority and sensing reliability limit the current design. In simulation, holding trim used approximately 84\% of the nose-down fin range (Section~\ref{sec:sim_results}); this identifies limited simulated descent margin, not a measured climbing margin. Experiment Six separately showed speed-dependent response: above about 2\,knots the rig struggled to dive, and below about 1\,knot it struggled to climb. The most promising regulation was observed near 1.5\,knots, but the complete operating envelope was not established. Widening that band requires a more detailed hydrodynamic analysis of the foil, fins and tow geometry than the simplified force model of Section~\ref{sec:sim_model}. The findings below are organised by research question.

\subsection{Research Question 1: Active Altitude Control Against a Passive Baseline}
\label{sec:conc_rq1}
Experiment One qualitatively supported a stable diving response at 1/7th scale, with no divergent pitch or yaw observed. Experiment Six provided qualitative evidence that roll and yaw could be handled passively during the tested conditions, supporting the decision to control pitch actively (Section~\ref{sec:activeStab}). A quantitative comparison of roll stability, as predicted in Table~\ref{tab:research_questions}, was not reported.

The prototype demonstrated ultrasonic-feedback altitude control in pool trials and one calm-water ocean session. In the pool, it approached and crossed a 400\,mm target without the repeated full-range oscillation seen in Experiment Five, although the run ended before sustained holding could be established. Active control was associated with a higher proportion of valid altitude measurements within the target band than the adjusted passive configuration. Different towing geometry, unequal run durations and the absence of an independent altitude reference limit attribution of that improvement to the controller. The altitude-regulation component of the hypothesis therefore has preliminary support; the full hypothesis has not been conclusively established. Reliable obstacle avoidance and operation across the intended speed range remain undemonstrated.

\subsection{Research Question 2: Obstacle Detection While Holding Imaging Altitude}
\label{sec:conc_rq2}
This question remains unanswered experimentally. No physical obstacle-clearance trial was completed in either the pool or the ocean. A manually commanded altitude step tested vertical response but did not test obstacle perception or automatic avoidance. The approximately 2\,m practical slant range observed in the ocean further restricts warning distance. At level pitch and 1\,m altitude, a $35^\circ$ beam intersects the seabed only 0.70\,m ahead, substantially short of the 2.5\,m look-ahead requirement.

The simulated ramp checks also failed to establish reliable avoidance: neither plant activated avoidance or reflex action, and the towed-foil case had not settled to the 1\,m target before reaching the ramp (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_sim_faults}). Clearance in those runs therefore does not demonstrate successful reactive avoidance from a settled survey condition.

There is also an imaging trade-off: pitching up to climb tilts the fixed camera away from the near-vertical view intended for mat-forming algae such as Caulerpa \parencite{cresswell}. Camera footage is linked in Appendix~\ref{sec:AppCompendium}, but image suitability was not quantified. Validation requires controlled obstacle approaches from a settled survey altitude, adequate sensing coverage and an explicit image-quality criterion.

\subsection{Research Question 3: Vertical Manoeuvres Within Rate Limits}
\label{sec:conc_rq3}
The specification requires a $20^\circ$ pitch-up response within about 1\,s (Section~\ref{design_specs}). Compliance has not been demonstrated. In Experiment Six, a 600\,mm altitude set-point step at 1\,knot took about 10\,s while the fins remained saturated nose-up. This establishes a slow altitude response at the tested speed, but does not directly measure the required pitch rate. The pitch trace must be analysed separately to determine time to the specified attitude and the achieved rate.

Tow speed, rope length and rope angle are plausible contributors to the response. Their effect on the rope's pitching moment follows from the attachment geometry in Section~\ref{tow_attach} and the signed moment balance in Equation~\eqref{eq:moment}. The empirical pitch-rate relationship in Equation~\eqref{eq:tow_pitch} is a simplified model, not an explicit torque calculation. The simulated nose-down trim margin cannot by itself explain the physical nose-up limitation. Fin geometry, available deflection and tow-point placement require further evaluation before claiming the specified manoeuvring capability.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:conc_limitations}
\begin{itemize}[itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Test environments.} Most trials ran in pools no deeper than 2\,m, which limited the target altitude to below the 1\,m design value and the run length to a few seconds. The ocean trial was a single session in calm conditions.
    \item \textbf{Tow speed.} Pool runs were towed by hand, with speed estimated from video, so speed varied within and between runs.
    \item \textbf{Experimental comparison.} The ocean results comprise one run per configuration with different rope lengths and unequal durations; controller effects cannot be isolated from towing geometry and environmental differences.
    \item \textbf{Altitude reference.} Errors were calculated from the rig's own estimate without an independent clearance measurement. Invalid samples represent unknown altitude, and short pool runs did not establish sustained holding.
    \item \textbf{Obstacles.} No physical obstacle-clearance trial was completed, and the simulated checks did not establish reliable avoidance.
    \item \textbf{Application requirements.} Image suitability, total prototype cost and multi-unit performance were not quantitatively evaluated in this report.
    \item \textbf{Simulation.} The plant gain $k_\delta$ was not fitted to the final rig, and the model omits the free surface, currents, cable catenary and roll and yaw dynamics (Section~\ref{sec:sim_results}).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Future Work}
\label{sec:conc_future}
\begin{itemize}[itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Controlled comparison.} Repeat active and fins-fixed runs over the same route with matched rope geometry and tow speed, recording the final hardware configuration. Use an independent altitude reference, report all-sample measurement availability and analyse measured pitch response against the manoeuvring requirement.
    \item \textbf{Sensing and authority.} Validate echo rejection and sensing range, then quantify nose-up and nose-down fin margins across tow speeds and rope angles before selecting changes to the fins or attachment geometry.
    \item \textbf{Open-water obstacle trials.} Test avoidance against known obstacles from a settled survey altitude, which is the end goal of the project. This needs a towing vessel that can hold a steady speed over a mapped site, which was not available during the testing period.
    \item \textbf{Parallel modules.} The design was built to allow several units to be towed together, but only a single unit was built and tested within the project timeframe. Towing multiple units would test the parallel-operation specification.
    \item \textbf{Custom PCB.} The electronics were assembled from separate modules with loose connections that were prone to breaking. A custom PCB would make the electronics enclosure smaller and more reliable.
\end{itemize}

\section{Simulation Model, Implementation and Supporting Results}
\label{sec:AppSim}
\setcounter{equation}{0}
\setcounter{figure}{0}
\setcounter{table}{0}
\setcounter{lstlisting}{0}

This appendix records the assumptions and supporting comparisons for Section~\ref{sec:sim}. The simulator calls the firmware control step every 20\,ms and advances the plant in 1\,ms steps. Two alternative plants are provided; they are not interchangeable calibrations of the physical rig.

\subsection{Plant Equations and Parameters}
\label{sec:app_sim_models}

Let $z$ be vertical position, positive upward, $z_b(x)$ seabed elevation, $h=z-z_b(x)$ clearance, $U$ prescribed forward speed, $\theta$ nose-up pitch and $\delta$ fin deflection. The code stores angular states in degrees and distances in millimetres, converting to radians and SI units for trigonometry and force calculations. The equations below use consistent physical units.

The generic plant represents pitch as a damped second-order response and makes flight-path angle $\gamma_f$ follow pitch:
\begin{align}
\ddot\theta&=\omega_n^2(k_f\delta-\theta)-2\zeta\omega_n\dot\theta,
&\omega_n&=2\frac{U}{U_{\mathrm{ref}}}\ \mathrm{rad/s},\\
\dot\gamma_f&=\frac{\theta-\gamma_f}{\tau_f},
&\dot z&=U\sin\gamma_f.
\end{align}
Here $k_f=1$, $\zeta=0.7$, $U_{\mathrm{ref}}=1$\,m/s and $\tau_f=0.3$\,s. This plant contains neither rope forces nor foil dimensions. It provides a separate comparison, rather than the towed-foil plant with a constant trim bias removed.

The towed-foil plant combines an empirical pitch-rate relationship with rope-angle restoration:
\begin{equation}
\dot\theta=k_\delta\delta-\frac{\theta-\theta_r}{\tau_r},
\qquad
\theta_r=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{H_T-h}{X_T}\right).
\label{eq:tow_pitch}
\end{equation}
The nominal tow point is $H_T$ above the local seabed and $X_T$ ahead. Pitching bias therefore changes with clearance and attitude. There is no explicit transport delay or constant fitted pitch-rate intercept in this equation. The generic plant's 0.3\,s flight-path lag and the fitting time shift in Section~\ref{sec:app_sim_fit} have separate roles.

Vertical motion follows the force balance
\begin{align}
(m+m_a)\ddot z&=F_L\cos\gamma_f-D\sin\gamma_f+F_{T,z}-(W-B),
\label{eq:sim_heave}\\
F_{T,z}&=(D\cos\gamma_f+F_L\sin\gamma_f)\tan\theta_r,
\end{align}
where $\gamma_f=\tan^{-1}(\dot z/U)$ and $\alpha=\theta-\gamma_f$ is angle of attack. The signed lift $F_L$ is positive upward, distinct from the earlier downward-force convention $L$. With $V_r^2=U^2+\dot z^2$, planform area $S=c_f b$ and aspect ratio $AR=b/c_f$,
\begin{align}
F_L&=\tfrac12\rho V_r^2S C_L,\\
D&=\tfrac12\rho V_r^2\left[S\left(C_{D0}+\frac{C_L^2}{\pi e_{\mathrm{ind}}AR}\right)+A_D\right],\\
m_a&=\rho\pi c_f^2b/4.
\end{align}
Here $A_D$ is the additional body drag area, including its drag coefficient. Before stall, the finite-aspect-ratio lift slope is $2\pi AR/(AR+2)$ per radian. Inverting the 5\% camber gives a zero-lift angle of $+2(0.05)$\,rad. Lift is linear within 14$^\circ$ of zero lift; beyond this it falls by 4\% of the peak per additional degree, to a minimum of 60\% of the peak. This is an assumed stall model, not a measured polar.

\begin{table}[H]

\centering
\small
\caption{Parameters used in the reported towed-foil simulations.}
\label{tab:sim_plant_parameters}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Parameter & Value \\
\midrule
Chord $c_f$, span $b$ and area $S$ & 0.30\,m, 0.80\,m and 0.24\,m$^2$ \\
Camber and orientation & 5\%, inverted \\
Water density $\rho$ & 1025\,kg/m$^3$ \\
Body mass $m$; net submerged weight $W-B$ & 8\,kg; 0\,N \\
Tow-point offsets $H_T$, $X_T$ & 3\,m, 7\,m \\

The rope angle is calculated from local clearance, so the nominal tow point moves with seabed elevation when terrain changes. The force balance does not include a free surface, cable catenary, current, or roll and yaw dynamics. These simplifications limit transfer to the rig, particularly for terrain response and operating-envelope predictions.

\subsection{Log-Based Pitch-Rate Fitting}
\label{sec:app_sim_fit}

The plotting script provides a fitting workflow using consecutive logged attitude samples. It estimates $q_i=(\theta_{i+1}-\theta_i)/\Delta t_i$ rather than relying on the sparsely sampled gyro. Both endpoints must satisfy $|\phi|<20^\circ$ and $|\theta|<45^\circ$; intervals longer than 1.2\,s or with $|q_i|>40^\circ$/s are discarded. These screens do not independently confirm steady towing.

The logged servo command is converted to logical fin deflection by subtracting neutral and dividing by six. Its mean $f_i$ is taken over the attitude interval shifted 0.3\,s earlier. Duration-weighted least squares then solves
\begin{equation}
\min_{k_\delta,c_q}\sum_i\Delta t_i\left(q_i-k_\delta f_i-c_q\right)^2.
\end{equation}
The shift is an identification assumption. When requested, the script can pass the fitted slope to the tow scenario; it does not insert the fitted intercept or a 0.3\,s delay into Equation~\eqref{eq:tow_pitch}. Figures~\ref{fig:LogCalc} and~\ref{fig:LogCalc2} illustrate the workflow on the Experiment Five log. All numerical comparisons reported here retain $k_\delta=0.52$; these illustrations are not a new calibration of the final rig.

\subsection{Sensor, Estimator and Controller Settings}
\label{sec:app_sim_control}

Sonar rays use each beam's mounting angle and true pitch to intersect the seabed. One beam is polled every 60\,ms. Range noise has 12\,mm standard deviation, failed transactions have probability 0.20 and maximum range is 5\,m. Near-field echoes of 50--100\,mm are injected only in the specified fault cases. IMU noise standard deviations are 0.2$^\circ$ in attitude and 0.05\,m/s$^2$ in vertical acceleration. Calibration errors, persistent bias, acoustic beam width and angle-dependent reflection losses are omitted.

The firmware uses 8$^\circ$ hysteresis when switching the selected downward beam on an end cap. Its Kalman measurement standard deviation is 30\,mm, a tuning value distinct from the simulator's 12\,mm injected range noise. Sample freshness, single assimilation of each contributing echo and the fallback behaviour are described in Section~\ref{sec:kalman}.

The altitude deadband is entered at $|e|\leq15$\,mm and exited above 25\,mm. Inside it, proportional error is zero but integral trim is retained. Integration uses error capped at $\pm100$\,mm and pauses when closing speed towards the target reaches 25\,mm/s, or when pitch or fin saturation would be driven further in the error direction. Avoidance and reflex action prevent additional nose-down integral accumulation. The integral contribution is limited to $\pm30^\circ$.

Normal fin-command slew is 8$^\circ$/s, increasing to 24$^\circ$/s during reflex action. The actuator model separately limits physical servo motion to 350 servo-degrees/s, with six servo-degrees per degree of fin motion. Holding rope angle constant and neglecting slew and saturation, the local inner-loop time constant is
\begin{equation}
\tau_{\mathrm{inner}}=\frac{1}{k_\delta K_\theta+1/\tau_r}\approx0.71\ \mathrm{s}.
\end{equation}
This excludes changing rope geometry and heave coupling. The corresponding local steady-pitch relation is
\begin{equation}
\delta_{\mathrm{trim}}=\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{trim}}-\theta_r}{k_\delta\tau_r}.
\end{equation}

Avoidance projects fresh sonar returns into forward and downward coordinates $(x_i,d_i)$ relative to the rig. In millimetres, clearance-line penetration and the requested altitude are
\begin{align}
p&=\max_{i:x_i>0}\left\{0,\ 400\ \mathrm{mm}-x_i\tan30^\circ-d_i\right\},\\
h_{\mathrm{request}}&=h_{\mathrm{cruise}}+\min(0.5p,1500\ \mathrm{mm}),
\end{align}
with $p=0$ when no eligible return exists. Penetration is held for 0.3\,s; the live setpoint rises at no more than 800\,mm/s and falls at no more than 100\,mm/s. Beams mounted at $35^\circ$ or $90^\circ$ separately trigger a reflex below 500\,mm range. The positive fin addition is proportional to range shortfall, capped at 10$^\circ$ and held for 0.2\,s. Neither path applies statistical innovation rejection.

\subsection{Error Metrics and Time Alignment}
\label{sec:app_sim_metrics}

Tracking error is $e_h=h_{\mathrm{true}}-h_{\mathrm{target}}$, positive above target. ``Final'' in Table~\ref{tab:gains} is the mean signed tracking error over the final 5\,s; ``lowest'' is the minimum tracking error over the complete run. Tracking RMS is $\sqrt{N^{-1}\sum_j e_{h,j}^2}$ over the final 10\,s. These windows include every recorded sample in the window, without selecting only samples near the target. They describe specified portions of a specified run; they are not independent of run duration or a substitute for repeated-run statistics.

Settling is the first entry into the $\pm50$\,mm band after which all subsequent samples remain inside it until the run ends. It is therefore an end-of-run criterion, not proof that the system remains settled indefinitely. The baseline settling sample has recorded time 28.58\,s.

The export stores controller estimates before advancing the body through the next 20\,ms period, and true state afterwards. The baseline settling sample therefore represents body-state time 28.60\,s. Estimation RMS is computed on matched samples where both raw and filtered clearance are available, using the preceding exported body state as the aligned reference; the first reference is the initial 2\,m clearance. This yields raw and filtered estimation RMS values of 11.33 and 7.95\,mm. Tracking metrics instead use the exported true clearance against the target and require no estimate-to-truth alignment. For the baseline, final-10\,s tracking RMS is 13.76\,mm, final-5\,s mean error is $+16.35$\,mm and minimum clearance is 981.09\,mm.

\subsection{Supplementary Sensitivity and Fault Checks}
\label{sec:app_sim_faults}
\label{sec:app_sim_checks}

Fin-authority checks used 120\,s towed-foil runs with the baseline initial clearance, target, speed and seed. At $k_\delta=0.05$, the fins saturated at $-25^\circ$ and final-5\,s mean altitude was 2.184\,m; at $k_\delta=1.0$, it was 0.995\,m. These are sensitivity choices, not confidence bounds from a verified fit. The simulator has no free surface, so values above a 2\,m pool depth indicate departure from the intended submerged operating condition.

Ramp checks used 35\,s runs starting at 1.5\,m, with a 1\,m target, 1\,m/s speed and seed 1. The bed rose 300\,mm over 600\,mm of track, starting 12\,m along the tow. Neither plant activated avoidance or reflex action. Generic minimum clearance was 675\,mm; towed-foil minimum was 975\,mm, but clearance at ramp entry was still 1.285\,m. This did not establish avoidance from a settled 1\,m towed-foil approach. At level pitch and 1\,m altitude, a $35^\circ$ beam meets the floor only 0.70\,m ahead, giving 0.70\,s at 1\,m/s against a 0.48\,s full sonar cycle.

False-echo checks used 40\,s runs starting at 1.8\,m, with a 1\,m target, 1\,m/s speed and seed 7. Injecting 50--100\,mm echoes with 3\% probability on otherwise successful, in-range transactions increased final-10\,s tracking RMS from 17.72 to 112.20\,mm on the generic plant and from 13.69 to 186.74\,mm on the towed foil. Final-5\,s mean errors changed from $+1.23$ to $+132.56$\,mm and from $-2.52$ to $+200.18$\,mm respectively. Avoidance and reflex action were active for approximately 15.2\% and 6.6\% of each fault run. Neither fault case remained within the $\pm50$\,mm band through the end. Echo validation is therefore needed in both the estimation and raw-range avoidance paths; its effectiveness was not tested here.
